## Topological Spaces

::: block
### Definition 2.1

Let $X$ be a non-empty set. A set $\tau$ of subsets of $X$ is said to be a **topology** on $X$ if:

\vspace{4mm}

\(i\) $X$ and the empty set, $\emptyset$, belong to $\tau$ (or simply $X,\emptyset\in\tau$),

\(ii\) The union of any collection of sets in $\tau$ belongs to $\tau$, and

\(iii\) The intersection of any finite collection of sets in $\tau$ belongs to $\tau$.

\vspace{4mm}

Then the pair $(X,\tau)$ is called a **topological space**.
:::

There are two things that make up a topological space;

a set, $X$, and a collection, $\tau$, of subsets of $X$,

that forms a topology on $X$.

## Topological Spaces - Examples

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Let $X = \{a,b,c\}$ and

$$\tau_1 = \{X,\emptyset,\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$$

Then $\tau_1$ is a topology on $X$ as it satisfies all those 3 conditions.
:::

## Open Set

::: block
### Definition 2.2

Let $(X,\tau)$ be any topological space. Then the members of $\tau$ are said to be **open sets**.
:::

::: block
### Proposition 2.3

If $(X,\tau)$ be any topological space, then:

\
(i) $X$ and $\emptyset$ are open sets,

\(ii\) The union of any collection of sets in $\tau$ is an open set, and

\(iii\) The intersection of any finite collection of sets in $\tau$ is an open set.
:::

Clearly this proposition is trivial consequences of the Definition in first slide.

## Discrete Topology

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Let $X$ be a non-empty set. Define $\tau$ be a collection of all subsets of $X$ or

$$\tau = \mathcal{P}(X)=\{U\,|\,U\subseteq X\}$$
:::

\vspace{2mm}

Clearly this is a topology, since unions and intersections of subsets of $X$ are themselves subset of $X$ and therefore are in $\tau$ (by definition of $\tau$ in the box above).

We call this the **discrete topology** on $X$, so then $(X,\tau)$ is a **discrete space**.

This is the **largest topology** that we can define on $X$.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Also, observe that $X$ can be any non-empty set. So there is an **infinite number** of discrete spaces - one for each set $X$.
:::

## Discrete Topology - Example

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Let $X = \{a,b,c\}$ and

$$\tau = \{X,\emptyset,\{a\},\{b\},\{c\},\{a,b\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\}\}$$

\vspace{2mm}

Then $\tau$ is a topology on $X$ as it satisfies all those 3 conditions,

and since $\tau$ contains all of possible subsets of $X$, we said $\tau$ is a discrete topology on $X$.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](week3/figure8.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
:::::

## Discrete Topology (cont.)

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If $X = \{a,b,c\}$ and $\tau$ is a topology on $X$ with $\{a\}\in\tau, \{b\}\in\tau\,\,\text{and}\,\,\{c\}\in\tau,$ then $\tau$ is a **discrete topology** on $X$.
:::

We already given that $\tau$ is a topology on $X$ so then it does satisfy **all three requirement** in the first definition.

In this case, it is given that $\tau$ contains every singleton set in $X$, which here is $\{a\},\{b\}\,\text{and}\,\{c\}$. By definition of topological space, any union and finite intersection of those singleton set, is also belong to $\tau$ which here is $\emptyset\,,\{a,b\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\},\{a,b,c\}=X$. Observed that $\tau$ actually already contains all the possible subset of $X$, which is the definition of the **discrete topology**.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
If $(X,\tau)$ is a topological space that, for every $x\in X$, the **singleton set** $\{x\}$ is in $\tau$, then $\tau$ is the **discrete topology**.
:::

## Indiscrete Topology

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Let $X$ be a non-empty set. Define

$$\tau = \{\emptyset,X\}$$
:::

\vspace{4mm}

Notice that $\tau$ satisfies all three of the conditions for being a topology, so it is a topology. However, if we remove either set, we no longer have a topology. \vspace{1mm}

Thus $\{\emptyset,X\}$ is the **minimal topology** we can define on $X$. \vspace{1mm}

For obvious reasons. it is called the **trivial topology** on $X$. \vspace{1mm}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
Also, it is called **indiscrete topology**, so then $(X,\tau)$ is said to be **indiscrete space**.
:::

## Discrete and Indiscrete Topology

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal"}
We can now realize that both discrete and indiscrete topology are the most extreme cases;

$$\{\emptyset,X\} \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$$
:::

Others interesting topology lie somewhere in the middle of them, and the number of topology available depends on how many elements in $X$;

\(i\) if $|X|=1$, for instance $X=\{a\}$, there is only one topology with discrete = indiscrete.

\(ii\) if $|X|=2$, for instance $X=\{a,b\}$, there are 4 different topology on $X$, which is $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\{\emptyset,X\},\{\emptyset,X,\{a\}\},\{\emptyset,X,b\}\}\,\,\text{and}\,\,\{\emptyset,X,\{a\},\{b\}\} = \mathcal{P}(X)$.

and it will increase quickly with $29$ choices for $|X|=3$, $355$ choices for $|X|=4$, $6942$ choices for $|X|=5$, $209 527$ choices for $|X|=6$, and so on

## Euclidean Topology

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A subset $S$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is said to be an open set in the euclidean topology, $\tau$, on $\mathbb{R}$, or $(\mathbb{R},\tau)$, if it has the following property:

For each $x \in S$, there exist $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, with $a<b$, such that $x\in (a,b)\subseteq S$.
:::

![](week3/figure5.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

Whenever we refer to the topological space $\mathbb{R}$ without specifying the topology, we mean $\mathbb{R}$ with the euclidean topology.

By that reason, it is also called the **standard topology** on $\mathbb{R}$.

There are several remarks for this euclidean topology:

## Euclidean Topology (cont.)

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
\(i\) The "euclidean topology, $\tau$, on $\mathbb{R}$", is a topology, and therefore $(\mathbb{R},\tau)$ is a topological space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
\(ii\) Every open interval is an open set in $\mathbb{R}$, but the converse not always true.
:::

For example, the set $(1,3)\bigcup (5,6)$ is an open set in $\mathbb{R}$, but it is not an open interval.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
\(iii\) For each $c,d\in\mathbb{R}$ with $c<d$, the closed interval $[c,d]$ is **not** an open set in $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

## Euclidean Topology (cont.)

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
\(iv\) Let $r,s\in\mathbb{R}$ with $r<s$. In the euclidean topology, $\tau$, on $\mathbb{R}$, the open interval $(r,s)$ does indeed belong to $\tau$, so it is an open set.
:::

To prove that $(r,s)$ is an open set, let's take any point $x \in (r,s)$. We need to find an open interval $(a,b)$ that contains $x$ and fits entirely inside $(r,s)$.

The simplest solution is to choose $(a,b)$ to be $(r,s)$ itself. Since the statement $x \in (r,s) \subseteq (r,s)$ is trivially true, it satisfies the definition perfectly.

![](week3/figure6.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

## Euclidean Topology (cont.)

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
\(v\) The open intervals $(-∞,r)$ and $(r,∞)$ are open sets in $\mathbb{R}$, for every real number $r$.
:::

For the set $(-\infty, r)$, let's take any point $x \in (-\infty, r)$, which means $x < r$. We need to construct a finite open interval $(a,b)$ around $x$ that sits completely inside the set.

We can simply set the lower limit $a = x-1$ and the upper limit $b = r$.

Since $x$ is clearly inside $(x-1, r)$, and the interval stops exactly at $r$, the condition $x \in (x-1, r) \subseteq (-\infty, r)$ is satisfied.

![](week3/figure7.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}
